findings.slide_ref: Ch1-2 - Introduction_1_.pptx, Slide 2 (and footer of every slide deck in the course)
findings.claim: Textbook cited as 'Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts – 9th Edition' (©2013); footer 'Operating System Concepts – 9th Edition' appears on virtually every slide.
findings.citation_excerpt: Welcome to the Web Page supporting Operating System Concepts, Tenth Edition. This new edition (April 15, 2018), which is published by John Wiley & Sons, is available for purchase…
findings.suggested_replacement: Adopt the 10th Edition (2018) of Operating System Concepts. The 10th edition revises terminology (e.g., 'NVM device' alongside HDD), updates examples (drops obsolete Solaris/Mac-OS-X references), and corrects sector-size guidance (512 B or 4,096 B). Update the footer and bibliographic citations accordingly.

findings.slide_ref: ch4 - Threads.pptx, Slide 12 ('Mac OS X iOS Android'); ch4 - Threads.pptx, Slide 20 ('Common in UNIX operating systems (Solaris, Linux & Mac OS X)'); Ch1-2 - Introduction_1_.pptx, Slide 17 ('POSIX API for POSIX-based systems (including … Mac OS X)')
findings.claim: Slides repeatedly refer to Apple's desktop operating system as 'Mac OS X'.
findings.citation_excerpt: With its debut on Mac, Siri is now on all four Apple software platforms — iOS, macOS, watchOS and tvOS… Apple today previewed macOS Sierra, a major update to the world's most advanced desktop operating system…
findings.suggested_replacement: Use the current name 'macOS' (rebranded from OS X / Mac OS X at WWDC 2016 with the release of macOS 10.12 Sierra). Where a historical context is intended, write 'macOS (formerly Mac OS X / OS X)'.

findings.slide_ref: ch4 - Threads.pptx, Slide 15 ('Many-to-One Model'): 'Few systems currently use this model: Solaris Green Threads, GNU Portable Threads'
findings.claim: Slide presents 'GNU Portable Threads' (and 'Solaris Green Threads') as current example implementations of the many-to-one threading model.
findings.citation_excerpt: Copyright © 1999-2006 Ralf S. Engelschall <rse@gnu.org>… Last Modified: 2006-06-08 20:20:09
findings.suggested_replacement: Drop 'GNU Portable Threads' as a current example — the project's last release (2.0.7) is from 8 June 2006 and the GNU page itself has not been updated since then; even GnuPG, its largest historical user, has migrated to a replacement (nPth) that wraps the system's native threads. 'Solaris Green Threads' was likewise removed from Solaris in the early 2000s. If a many-to-one example is needed, present it as historical (e.g., 'early Solaris (Green Threads, removed in Solaris 9, 2002), early Java threads on Linux (Green Threads, removed when LinuxThreads/NPTL became standard)') and note that essentially all general-purpose OSes today use the one-to-one model.

findings.claim: 'I/O transfers performed in blocks of sectors (usually 512 bytes)'.
findings.citation_excerpt: Storage devices may report a physical block size that is bigger than the logical block size (for instance a drive with 4KB physical sectors exposing 512-byte logical blocks to the operating system).
findings.suggested_replacement: State that modern storage devices use either 512-byte or 4,096-byte (4 KiB / 'Advanced Format') sectors, and that solid-state / NVM devices essentially always use 4 KiB blocks. (The 10th-edition speaker notes already say this — 'Depending on the disk drive, sector size is usually 512 bytes or 4,096 bytes. NVM devices usually have blocks of 4,096 bytes' — but the slide text was not updated to match.) Also distinguish 'logical block size' (often still 512 B for compatibility) from 'physical block size' (commonly 4 KiB).
